title: How life began: the oldest life and the RNA idea

summary.text: Every living thing comes from another living thing. So how did the very first life begin? Nobody knows for sure yet. The Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. The oldest signs of life we have found are rocks about 3.5 billion years old, built in layers by mats of tiny microbes. These rocks are called stromatolites, and some are found in India too. Before life, the young sea held simple chemicals. Experiments show that some of the building blocks of life can form from these chemicals without any living thing. Many scientists think the first life was RNA, a chain molecule that can carry instructions and can also help make copies of itself. Later, tiny green microbes began to make oxygen. Their oxygen rusted the iron in the sea and changed the air for ever.
summary.art: A long ribbon of time across a page: on the left a young, steaming Earth with a dark sea, then domed striped rocks in shallow water, then a sea turning rusty red, and at the far right end a tiny child holding a magnifying glass.

intro.hook: You came from your mother. She came from her mother, and so on, back and back. A curry leaf plant came from a seed, which came from another curry leaf plant. Every living thing comes from another living thing. So where did the very first living thing come from, when there was nothing alive to come from?
intro.text: This is one of the biggest questions in science, and it is still open. In this unit you meet the oldest life we know, which left striped rocks behind. You test what the first oxygen did to iron, with nails in jars of water. You see the white threads of DNA from a banana. And you learn the leading idea about how life began: the RNA idea. Scientists are still testing it, and you can weigh the evidence too.
intro.art: A child at a window, holding up a curry leaf, with a dotted line going back from the leaf to a seed, to an older plant, and on into a misty sea with a question mark in it.

outcomes: I can say that every living thing comes from another living thing, and explain why that makes the first life a puzzle.
I can say when the Earth formed and how old the oldest signs of life are, and place them on a timeline made to scale.
I can explain what stromatolites are and how tiny microbes built them in layers.
I can run a fair test with iron nails in water, and use it to explain how the first oxygen made by microbes rusted the iron in the sea.
I can explain that RNA is a chain of four kinds of letters that can carry instructions, and show how a chain is copied by matching pairs.
I can describe the RNA idea, and say why it is still an idea that scientists are testing.
I can tell how Wöhler and Miller showed that the chemicals of life can form without a living thing.
I can name the main ideas about where life began, and say that nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: The smallest living unit. Every living thing is made of one cell or many cells. Each cell has a thin skin around a watery inside.
terms.example: A bacterium is one cell. Your body is made of tens of trillions of cells.
terms.art: A round cell with a thin skin, a watery inside and a tangle of thread in the middle.

terms.meaning: A living thing too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria are microbes.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are microbes.
terms.art: A drop of water under a magnifying glass, full of tiny rod-shaped and round microbes.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of atoms joined together. Everything around you is made of molecules.
terms.example: Water is made of water molecules. Each one is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
terms.art: Three balls stuck together, one big and two small, labelled 'a water molecule'.

terms.meaning: A thousand million. Written out, it is 1 followed by 9 zeros: 1,000,000,000.
terms.example: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. In Indian numbers, one billion is 100 crore.
terms.art: A row of 1 followed by nine zeros, with the words 'one thousand million'.

terms.meaning: Any trace of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock. It can be a bone, a shell, a print, or a shape left by tiny living things.
terms.example: A shell turned to stone, or a dinosaur footprint, is a fossil.
terms.art: A grey stone with the shape of a spiral shell pressed into it.

terms.meaning: A rock built up in thin layers by mats of microbes in shallow water. The microbes trap mud and sand, then grow up through it, again and again.
terms.example: Stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old are found in Western Australia. Ones about 2 billion years old are found near Vempalle, in the Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh.
terms.art: A cut-open dome of rock showing many thin wavy layers, like the inside of a stack of dosas.

terms.meaning: Tiny bacteria that make their food from sunlight, water and air, as plants do. As they do this, they give out oxygen.
terms.example: The dark green or black film on a damp wall in the monsoon often holds cyanobacteria.
terms.art: A thread of tiny green beads, with little bubbles of oxygen rising from it.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that we need to breathe. Almost all of it was made by living things that use sunlight, such as cyanobacteria, algae and plants.
terms.example: Every breath you take brings oxygen into your body.
terms.art: A child breathing in, with small O shapes floating into her nose from a green leaf.

terms.meaning: The orange-brown stuff that forms when iron joins with oxygen. Water helps rust form.
terms.example: An old iron gate that stays out in the rain turns rusty.
terms.art: An iron nail half grey and half covered in orange-brown rust.

terms.meaning: A very long chain molecule inside every cell. It holds the instructions for building and running that living thing. Its chain uses four kinds of chemical letters.
terms.example: Your DNA came half from your mother and half from your father.
terms.art: A twisted ladder with four colours of rungs.

terms.meaning: A chain molecule, a close cousin of DNA. Its four chemical letters are called A, U, C and G. In every cell, RNA carries copies of instructions from the DNA and helps build proteins.
terms.example: In your cells, RNA copies of instructions travel from the DNA to the cell's protein-building machines.
terms.art: A single wiggly strand with beads in four colours, labelled A, U, C and G.

terms.meaning: A molecule made of a chain of smaller molecules called amino acids, folded into a shape. Proteins do most of the work in a cell.
terms.example: Your hair and nails are mostly a protein called keratin. Dal is rich in protein.
terms.art: A long chain of beads folding up into a knotted ball.

terms.meaning: A small molecule. Living things join amino acids into chains to make proteins.
terms.example: Stanley Miller made amino acids in a glass flask with gases, water and electric sparks.
terms.art: A small bead with a tag on it, joining a chain of other beads.

terms.meaning: A piece of RNA that does a job in the cell, such as cutting or joining other molecules. It is RNA acting like a tool.
terms.example: Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman found ribozymes in the early 1980s.
terms.art: A strand of RNA folded into a hook shape, holding two small molecules together.

terms.meaning: A crack in the sea floor where hot water full of minerals pours out from deep inside the Earth.
terms.example: Vents were first seen in 1977, deep in the Pacific Ocean near the Galápagos Islands.
terms.art: A tall chimney on a dark sea floor puffing out black, smoky water, with shrimps and worms around it.

terms.meaning: A rock from space that falls to the ground on Earth.
terms.example: The Murchison meteorite fell in Australia in 1969. It holds amino acids that formed in space.
terms.art: A dark, lumpy stone lying in a small dent in the ground.

terms.meaning: An idea that tries to explain something, and that can be tested.
terms.example: 'Life began as RNA' is a hypothesis. Scientists test it with experiments.
terms.art: A child with a speech bubble that says 'I think...' and a test tube in her hand.

terms.meaning: A living being that someone came from, long ago. Your grandmothers and great-grandmothers are your ancestors.
terms.example: All living things today share very old ancestors: the first cells.
terms.art: A family tree drawn as a banyan tree, with a small round cell at the bottom of the trunk.

explanations.concept: Every living thing comes from another living thing
explanations.definition: Today, every living thing comes from another living thing of its own kind. A cell comes only from another cell.
explanations.description: Puppies come from dogs. A mango tree grows from a mango seed, and the seed came from another mango tree. Even bacteria come only from other bacteria, by splitting in two. Scientists tested this for hundreds of years, and it has always held. That is what makes the first life such a puzzle. If life comes only from life, how did the first life begin? Something must once have been different.
examples: You came from your parents, and they came from theirs.
Curd sets only when you add a little old curd, because the curd bacteria come from other curd bacteria.
explanations.art: A chain of mothers and babies going back: a girl, her mother, a grandmother, then a monkey-like ancestor, then a fish, then a single round cell at the end.
explanations.context: This card says why the first life is a puzzle.

explanations.definition: The Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. It had oceans of liquid water by about 4.4 billion years ago. The air then had almost no oxygen.
explanations.description: At first the Earth was very hot, and rocks from space crashed into it often. As it cooled, water fell as rain and filled the oceans. We know there was liquid water very early because of tiny crystals called zircons, found in Western Australia. Some are about 4.4 billion years old, and their chemistry shows they formed with water around. The young sea had no fish, no seaweed and no living thing at all. It held salts, iron, and simple chemicals made of carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen.
examples: Zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old.
A 4.5 metre time string, with one metre for each billion years, shows how long the Earth had no life.
explanations.art: A young Earth seen from space: dark seas, smoking volcanoes on small islands, and a big Moon close in the sky.
explanations.context: This card is about what the Earth was like before there was any life.

explanations.concept: The oldest life we know: stromatolites
explanations.definition: Stromatolites are rocks built in layers by mats of microbes in shallow water. The oldest ones we are fairly sure of are about 3.5 billion years old.
explanations.description: A mat of microbes is a slimy carpet of millions of tiny living things. Mud and sand settle on the mat and stick to it. The microbes then grow up through the mud towards the light, and make a new mat on top. Year after year, this builds up a dome of thin layers. Over time the domes turn to stone. The oldest stromatolites we know are in the Pilbara, in Western Australia. Abigail Allwood, an Australian geologist, and her team showed in 2006 that a reef there, about 3.4 billion years old, was built by living things. Living stromatolites still grow today at Shark Bay, in Australia, where the water is too salty for snails that would eat the mats.
examples: Stromatolites about 2 billion years old are found near Vempalle in the Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh.
Jhamarkotra near Udaipur and Bhojunda near Chittorgarh, in Rajasthan, are stromatolite parks you can visit.
explanations.art: A row of living stromatolite domes, like grey cushions, sticking out of clear shallow water at Shark Bay, with a cut-open one beside it showing its layers.
explanations.context: This card is about the oldest life we have found signs of, and how they left those signs.

explanations.concept: How the first oxygen rusted the sea
explanations.definition: Cyanobacteria were among the first living things to make oxygen. Their oxygen joined with iron in the sea and made rust, which sank in layers. Later the oxygen filled the air.
explanations.description: Iron rusts only when oxygen reaches it. The young sea had almost no oxygen, so iron could stay dissolved in the water, the way salt stays dissolved. Then cyanobacteria began making oxygen from sunlight and water. Where their oxygen met the iron, rust formed and settled on the sea floor. Layer after layer, it made striped rocks called banded iron formations. Most scientists think much of this rust formed because of the microbes. By about 2.4 billion years ago, the extra oxygen also began to fill the air. Scientists call this the Great Oxidation Event. Much of the iron ore mined in India, at Kudremukh, Sandur and Bailadila, comes from banded iron rocks.
examples: In the nail test, the nail in open water rusted, but the nail sealed under oil stayed almost shiny.
Banded iron rock has red stripes of rust between grey or black stripes.
explanations.art: A cut piece of rock with red and grey stripes, and above it a sea where green microbes give out bubbles that turn the water rusty.
explanations.context: This card explains what the first oxygen did, and what the nail test tells us about it.

explanations.concept: The building blocks of life can form without life
explanations.definition: Some molecules that living things are made of, such as amino acids, can form from simple chemicals with no living thing involved.
explanations.description: People once thought that only living things could make the chemicals of life. In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a chemical found in urine, from chemicals that were not alive. In 1952, Stanley Miller filled a glass flask with water and the gases methane, ammonia and hydrogen. He made electric sparks in it, like lightning, for a week. The water turned brown, and in it he found amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Amino acids have also been found in meteorites, such as the Murchison meteorite that fell in Australia in 1969. In 2008, Zita Martins and her team found uracil, one of the letters of RNA, in the same meteorite.
examples: Miller's flask made the amino acid glycine, which is also in your body.
Meteorites show that some building blocks of life form even in space.
explanations.art: A glass flask of brownish water with two metal points making a spark, and the words 'amino acids' written beside it.
explanations.context: This card is about the experiments that showed life's chemicals can be made without life.

explanations.concept: RNA: a chain of four letters
explanations.definition: RNA is a chain molecule. Its chain is made of four kinds of small parts, written as A, U, C and G. The order of the letters can carry instructions.
explanations.description: Think of a long bead necklace with beads in four colours. The order of the colours is a message. RNA is like that, but the beads are molecules. The letters also pair up: A pairs with U, and C pairs with G. So a chain can attract loose letters to make a partner chain, letter by letter. Copy the partner, and you get the first chain back. DNA works in the same way, with T in place of U. In your cells today, RNA carries copies of instructions from the DNA to the cell's protein-building machines.
examples: The chain A-U-G-C has the partner chain U-A-C-G.
Copy the partner U-A-C-G again, and you get A-U-G-C back.
explanations.art: Two strips of paper side by side, one with A U G C and the other with U A C G, with lines joining the pairs.
explanations.context: This card is about what RNA is and how its letters pair up to make copies.

explanations.definition: Some RNA molecules fold into shapes that do jobs, such as cutting or joining other molecules. These are called ribozymes.
explanations.description: For a long time, scientists thought only proteins could do the jobs in a cell. Then, in the early 1980s, Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman found RNA molecules that do jobs too. They won the Nobel Prize in 1989. Then came an even bigger find. Every cell has machines called ribosomes, which join amino acids into proteins. In 2000, scientists showed that the part of the ribosome that does the joining is made of RNA, not protein. Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, born in Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, Ada Yonath from Israel and Thomas Steitz from the United States worked out the ribosome's shape. They won the Nobel Prize in 2009. Ada Yonath worked on it for about 20 years, while many scientists said it could not be done.
examples: Every protein in your body was put together by ribosomes, at a working centre made of RNA.
Some medicines kill harmful bacteria by jamming their ribosomes.
explanations.art: A ribosome drawn as two lumpy halves, with an RNA strand threading through and a chain of beads coming out of the top.
explanations.context: This card is about RNA that does jobs, which is a big clue in the RNA idea.

explanations.description: This is an idea, not a settled fact. In every cell today, DNA holds the instructions, and proteins do most of the work. But each needs the other: proteins are needed to copy DNA, and DNA is needed to make proteins. So which came first? RNA can do both jobs. It can carry instructions, like DNA, and some RNA can do jobs, like proteins. So many scientists think the first life was RNA that could help copy itself. Later, DNA took over keeping the instructions, and proteins took over most of the jobs. Francis Crick, Leslie Orgel and Carl Woese suggested this in the 1960s, and Walter Gilbert named it 'the RNA world' in 1986. In 2009, Tracey Lincoln and Gerald Joyce made two RNA molecules in the lab that copy each other. But nobody has yet made RNA that copies itself from scratch, the way the idea needs.
examples: The ribosome's working centre is made of RNA, which may be left over from an RNA world.
In the lab, RNA molecules can be made that join other RNA pieces together.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour the RNA idea
perspectives.explanation: RNA can carry instructions and do jobs, and the ribosome's working centre is made of RNA. So RNA could have come before DNA and proteins.
RNA is hard to make and breaks easily. They think chains of chemical reactions, maybe on mineral surfaces at vents, came first, and RNA came later.

explanations.art: A chicken and an egg with a question mark between them, and next to them a strand of RNA holding both a message scroll and a tiny tool.
explanations.context: This card is about the leading idea of how life began. It is still being tested.

explanations.concept: Cell skins that form by themselves
explanations.definition: Molecules called fatty acids can gather in water to make tiny hollow bubbles with a thin skin. Many scientists think the first cells had skins like these.
explanations.description: A fatty acid molecule has one end that mixes with water and one end that stays away from water. In water, many of them line up side by side, with their water-shy ends tucked in. They close up into tiny hollow bubbles, each with a skin two molecules thick. In 1985, David Deamer showed that fatty acids taken from the Murchison meteorite form bubbles like these. In 2003, Jack Szostak's team showed that clay helps these bubbles form, and that RNA can stick to the same clay. A bubble with RNA inside might have been the first cell. Soap is made from fatty acids too.
examples: Soap bubbles get their thin skin from soap molecules lining up.
A cell's skin today is made of similar molecules, called lipids.
explanations.art: Tiny round bubbles in water, each with a skin of little pins lined up with their heads out, and one bubble holding a short RNA strand.
explanations.context: This card is about how the first cells might have got their skins.

explanations.concept: Copying with small mistakes makes new kinds
explanations.definition: When a chain is copied, a few letters sometimes come out wrong. These changes are called mutations. Copies that last and copy well become more common.
explanations.description: No copying is perfect. If a copy has one changed letter, its own copies carry that change too. Most changes make no difference, and some make a copy worse. A few make a copy better at lasting or copying. Over many copies, the better ones become more common. This is how one kind of life slowly becomes many kinds. It still happens today, in every living thing. Cells now have ways to check and fix their copies, so their mistakes are very rare.
examples: Bacteria that change in a way that lets them survive a medicine become more common in a body that takes the medicine.
In the copy-mistakes activity, a chain copied ten times ends up with letters that differ from the first chain.
explanations.art: A row of RNA strands, each copied from the one before, with one letter changing colour along the way.
explanations.context: This card is about how copying with small mistakes can make new kinds of life.

explanations.description: Nobody knows where life began. There are a few main ideas, and each has some evidence for it.
examples: At hot vents on the sea floor, where hot water full of minerals meets cold sea.
In warm pools on land, which fill with rain and dry out again and again.
Some think life, or its building blocks, came from space.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour sea-floor vents, such as Michael Russell and Nick Lane
perspectives.explanation: Vents give warmth, minerals and a steady flow of energy. Deborah Kelley found a field of vents called the Lost City in 2000, and its chemistry may be like that of the first life.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour warm pools on land, such as David Deamer and John Sutherland
perspectives.explanation: On land, pools dry out and fill up again. Drying helps small molecules join into chains, and fatty acid bubbles form well in fresh water. Charles Darwin guessed a 'warm little pond' in a letter in 1871.

perspectives.who: A few scientists, such as Fred Hoyle and Chandra Wickramasinghe
perspectives.explanation: They suggested that life itself came to Earth from space. Most scientists do not accept this. It would also not explain how life began in the first place.

explanations.art: Three pictures side by side: a smoking chimney on a dark sea floor, a steaming pool on a volcanic island, and a meteorite falling through the sky.
explanations.context: This card gives the main ideas about where life began. Scientists still argue about them.

explanations.definition: All living things today share the same ancestors, far back in time. Scientists call the most recent ancestor of all life today LUCA, the Last Universal Common Ancestor.
explanations.description: Bacteria, mushrooms, mango trees, crows and you all use DNA. All use RNA to carry instructions, and ribosomes to build proteins. All read the same three-letter code to choose amino acids. It is very unlikely that all of this matched by chance. So scientists agree that all life today comes from one shared family of early cells. Nobody knows exactly when LUCA lived. It was probably more than 3.5 billion years ago.
examples: Your cells and a banana's cells both hold DNA, as the banana DNA test shows.
A bacterium's ribosome and your ribosome are built in a very similar way.
explanations.art: A huge family tree with bacteria, mushrooms, plants, birds, fish and people on its branches, all growing from one small trunk with a round cell at its root.
explanations.context: This card is about why scientists say all life is one family.

agreed.text: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure the age of rocks and meteorites from the slow, steady change of some atoms into others, called radioactive decay.

agreed.text: Life has been on Earth for at least 3.5 billion years.
agreed.evidence: Stromatolites and the chemistry of very old rocks in Australia, and later ones in South Africa, India and elsewhere.

agreed.text: The first life was made of single cells, and it lived in water.
agreed.evidence: The oldest fossils are all of microbes. Fossils of animals with many cells come much later, in the last 600 million years or so.

agreed.text: Oxygen in the air was made by living things that use sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Very old rocks show no sign of oxygen in the air. Rocks younger than about 2.4 billion years show it. Banded iron rocks record when oxygen met iron in the sea.

agreed.text: Some building blocks of life can form without living things.
agreed.evidence: Miller's spark experiment, many later lab experiments, and amino acids and RNA letters found in meteorites.

agreed.text: All living things today share the same ancestors.
agreed.evidence: All life uses DNA, RNA, ribosomes and the same genetic code.

challenging.claim: Only living things can make the chemicals of life.
challenging.for: For a long time, nobody could make sugar, urea or other chemicals of living bodies in the lab.
challenging.against: Wöhler made urea in 1828, and Miller made amino acids in 1952. Chemists now make many such chemicals from non-living ones.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that experiments showed to be wrong.

challenging.claim: Life began as RNA, before DNA and proteins.
challenging.who: Many scientists who study how life began
challenging.for: RNA can carry instructions and do jobs, and the ribosome's working centre is made of RNA.
challenging.against: RNA is hard to make without a cell, and it breaks easily. Nobody has yet made RNA that copies itself from scratch.
challenging.context: This card is about the leading idea of how life began.

challenging.claim: Life began at hot vents on the sea floor.
challenging.who: Michael Russell, Nick Lane and others
challenging.for: Vents give warmth, minerals and energy, all day and night, safe from the harsh light of the young Sun.
challenging.against: RNA and other chains break apart easily in hot water, and vents do not dry out, so it is hard to join small pieces into long chains there.
challenging.context: This card is about one idea of where life began.

challenging.claim: Life began in warm pools on land.
challenging.who: David Deamer, John Sutherland and others
challenging.for: Pools dry and wet again, which helps small pieces join into chains. Lab chemistry with sunlight makes RNA letters.
challenging.against: There was little dry land on the young Earth, and we have no rocks from the first pools.
challenging.context: This card is about another idea of where life began.

challenging.claim: Life came to Earth from space.
challenging.who: Svante Arrhenius in 1903, and later Fred Hoyle and Chandra Wickramasinghe
challenging.for: Meteorites carry amino acids and RNA letters, and some microbes can survive a long time in space.
challenging.against: No living thing has ever been found in a meteorite. And the idea only moves the question: how did life begin out there?
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that life came from space.

challenging.claim: All life today comes from one shared family of early cells.
challenging.for: All living things use DNA, RNA, ribosomes and the same genetic code.
challenging.against: Some think life may have begun more than once, and the other kinds died out. Even so, all life alive today shares one family.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that all life is one family.

big_questions.q: If a chain of RNA could copy itself in the sea, would that chain be alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about what living things do. Which of those things would the chain do, and which would it not?

big_questions.q: Did life begin only once on Earth, or many times?
big_questions.hint: All life today shares one family. Could other kinds have begun and died out without leaving fossils?

big_questions.q: The first oxygen rusted the sea and changed the air. Is the Earth just a home for life, or partly made by life?
big_questions.hint: Think about the iron ore, the air you breathe and the soil in a flowerpot.

big_questions.q: Every cell comes from a cell. If we follow your cells back, where does the chain end?
big_questions.hint: Your mother's cells, her mother's cells, and on back for more than 3.5 billion years.

big_questions.q: Is there life on other worlds, such as Mars or the moons of Jupiter and Saturn?
big_questions.hint: If life began easily here, could it begin wherever there is water and energy?

big_questions.q: Could people one day make life from chemicals in a lab? If they did, how would we know it was alive?
big_questions.hint: What would the new thing need to do?

story.title: The Stripes in the Hill
story.note: Stromatolites about 2 billion years old really are found near Vempalle in the Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh, and banded iron rock really is found near Sandur in Karnataka. Nila, Karthik, Revathi and this trip are made up.
text: Nila was nine, and her brother Karthik was seven. In the summer holidays they went to stay with their aunt, Revathi Athai, in Kadapa. Athai was a geologist. That means she studied rocks. Her house was full of them. There were rocks on the shelves, rocks on the windowsills, and one big striped rock that held the bathroom door open.
"Tomorrow," said Athai at dinner, "I'll show you the oldest living thing you have ever seen." Karthik stopped eating his curd rice. "A tortoise?" he asked. "A banyan tree?" Athai only smiled.

Early the next morning, they drove out past fields of groundnut to a low grey hill near Vempalle. There were no trees on the hill, only rock. Athai walked along slowly, looking down. Then she knelt and brushed away some dust with her hand. "Here," she said.

Nila looked. The rock had thin wavy lines in it, hundreds of them, one on top of the other. In some places the lines curved up into little domes, like the tops of mushrooms. "It looks like a stack of dosas," said Karthik. Athai laughed. "It does. But a living thing made this."

"These are called stromatolites," Athai said. "About two billion years ago, this hill was the floor of a warm, shallow sea. On the sea floor lived a slimy mat of microbes, too small to see one by one. Mud settled on the mat. The microbes grew up through the mud towards the sunlight, and made a new mat on top. Then more mud came, and they grew up again." She ran her finger along one line. "Each of these lines is one layer of that mat."

"So the microbes are still in there?" asked Karthik. "Their bodies are long gone," said Athai. "But the shape of their work is kept in the stone. It is like a footprint in dried mud. The foot has gone, but you can still see where it was."

Nila counted the lines on one dome. She got to forty and lost count. "Two billion years," she said quietly. "Is that the oldest life there is?" "Not quite," said Athai. "In Australia there are stromatolites about three and a half billion years old. They are the oldest signs of life we are fairly sure of."

That evening, Athai took the big striped rock from the bathroom door and put it on the table. It had stripes of rusty red and stripes of shiny dark grey. "This one is from Sandur, in Karnataka," she said. "It is called banded iron. The red stripes are rust."

"Rust? Like on our gate?" asked Karthik. "Exactly like that," said Athai. "Long ago, the sea had almost no oxygen in it. Iron could stay in the water without rusting. Then microbes like the ones in the hill began to make oxygen from sunlight. Their oxygen met the iron, and rust formed. It sank to the sea floor in layers. So the microbes did not only make the stromatolites. They changed the whole sea, and in the end the air too. The oxygen you are breathing now was made by living things."

Karthik took a big breath and held it, as if it might run away. Nila was still thinking. "Athai," she said, "the microbes came from other microbes, right? Like curd comes from curd. But who did the very first microbes come from?"

Athai was quiet for a moment. Then she got up and fetched a pencil and a strip of paper. She wrote four letters on it: A, U, C, G. "Nobody knows yet," she said. "That is the honest answer. But here is one idea that many scientists like. Inside every cell there is a chain molecule called RNA. Its chain is made of four kinds of letters. And the letters pair up: A with U, and C with G."

She wrote a short chain: A U G C. Under it, she wrote the partners: U A C G. "Look. The first chain can make a partner chain, letter by letter. Copy the partner, and you get the first chain back. So a chain like this can make copies of itself, with a little help from the chemicals around it. Some RNA can also do jobs, like a tiny tool. Many scientists think life began as chains of RNA in the young sea, copying themselves."

"Did that really happen?" asked Karthik. "We don't know," said Athai. "Scientists are testing it. They have made some pieces of it work in the lab, but not the whole thing yet. Maybe one of you will find out."

Nila took the pencil and wrote a chain of her own. Then she made its partner, and the partner's partner. Her third chain matched her first one exactly, except for one letter, where she had written C instead of G. "Oops," she said. "A mistake."

"Keep it," said Athai. "Mistakes like that are how one kind of life slowly becomes many kinds." Nila looked at the striped rock, and at her paper chain, and at her brother, who was still holding his breath. "Breathe out, Karthik," she said. "The microbes will make more."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the wavy lines in the hill are stromatolites, layers built by mats of microbes that trapped mud and grew up through it. The red stripes in the banded iron are rust that formed when the first oxygen, made by microbes, met iron dissolved in the sea. The paper chain shows how RNA letters pair up, A with U and C with G, so that a chain can make a partner and the partner can make the first chain again. Nila's mistake shows how copies slowly change. Athai's honest answer is the real state of science: the RNA idea is a hypothesis, still being tested.
ask: How did tiny microbes make the wavy lines in the rock?
What are the red stripes in the banded iron rock, and how did they form?
Why could iron stay in the young sea without rusting?
Nila's third chain had one letter wrong. Why did Athai say to keep it?
Athai said 'Nobody knows yet.' Why is it good for a scientist to say that when it is true?

games.title: Copy Race: build the partner chain
games.context: This is a card game about how RNA is copied. Each player has a chain, and races to build its partner chain by the pairing rule: A with U, and C with G.

printables.title: 6 chain cards
items: A U G C C A
G G C A U U
C A U G A C
U U A G C G
A C G U G A
G C A U C U

rules: Shuffle the letter cards and put them face down in a pile.
Each player takes one chain card and lays it face up.
On your turn, take the top letter card. If it is the partner of your next letter, lay it under that letter. If not, put it on a discard pile.
A pairs with U. C pairs with G.
The first player to finish the whole partner chain wins.
Playing alone: time yourself. Try to beat your time with a new chain card.

flow.do: Shuffle the letter cards. Give each player a chain card.
flow.say: Each of you is a chain of RNA. You need to build your partner chain from the letters floating around.
flow.kid: Take a chain card. You are a chain of RNA. Build your partner chain.

flow.do: Play until someone finishes their partner chain.
flow.say: Remember: A goes with U, C goes with G. You can only place the partner of your next letter.
flow.kid: Take a card. Is it the partner of your next letter? Place it. If not, throw it away.
flow.parent: If the pile runs out, shuffle the discards and use them again. This is a little like RNA letters floating in the sea, waiting to be picked up.

flow.do: After the game, check every partner chain together.
flow.say: Let's check each chain. Did anyone place a wrong partner?
flow.kid: Check your partner chain. Is every pair right?

check.q: In Copy Race, Lakshmi's chain starts G G C. Which cards does she need for her partner chain, in order?
check.why: G pairs with C, and C pairs with G. So G G C needs C C G. Picking U U A mixes up the rules: U is the partner of A, not of G.

setup.caption: 2. Place each partner under its letter. First to finish wins.

games.title: Line Up Time: put the story of life in order
games.context: This is a card game about the order of events in the story of life. Players place event cards in order on a line, and earn points for each card placed right.

printables.title: 10 event cards
items: The Earth forms (4.5 billion years ago)
The first oceans (about 4.4 billion years ago)
The oldest stromatolites (about 3.5 billion years ago)
Oxygen starts to fill the air (about 2.4 billion years ago)
Stromatolites grow at Vempalle, in India (about 2 billion years ago)
The first animals (about 600 million years ago)
The first land plants (about 470 million years ago)
Dinosaurs die out (66 million years ago)
The first people like us (about 300,000 years ago)

rules: Put 'The Earth forms' at the start of the line, face up.
Shuffle the other cards with their dates covered, and deal them out.
On your turn, place one card on the line where you think it goes, then show its date.
If it is in the right place, score a point. If not, move it to the right place.
Playing alone: place all the cards, then check the dates and count how many you got right.

flow.do: Cover the dates on the cards with a strip of paper. Put 'The Earth forms' down first.
flow.say: These cards are events in the story of life. We have to put them in order, oldest first.
flow.kid: These are events in the story of life. Put them in order, oldest first.

flow.do: Take turns placing cards and checking the dates.
flow.say: Where does this one go? Before or after the stromatolites?
flow.kid: Place your card. Before or after the others? Then check its date.
flow.parent: The hardest ones are usually oxygen and animals. Many children put animals much earlier than they came. That surprise is the point.

flow.do: Count the points.
flow.say: What surprised you most about the order?
flow.kid: Count your points. What surprised you most?

options: Oxygen starts to fill the air
check.why: Oxygen began to fill the air about 2.4 billion years ago. The first animals came about 600 million years ago, which is much later. Dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago. Many people think animals came soon after the first life, but for most of Earth's story the only life was tiny.

experiments.title: The Rusting Nails: what did the first oxygen do to the sea?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put iron nails in three jars of water. In one jar, you keep oxygen away from the nail. Over three days you find out what oxygen does to iron, the way the first oxygen made by microbes did to the iron in the young sea.
experiments.question: Does an iron nail in water rust when very little oxygen can reach it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which nail will rust most: the nail in open tap water, the nail in boiled water sealed under oil, or the nail in open salty water? Which will rust least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three nails of the same kind and size, three jars of the same size, and the same amount of water in each. Keep the jars side by side in the same place. Only one thing changes in each jar: open water, water with little oxygen, or salty water.

materials.item: plain grey iron nails, about 5 cm long, all the same kind. Shiny silver nails have a zinc coat and rust slowly. If you only have shiny ones, rub them well with sandpaper or a rough stone first.
small clear glass jars or glasses, the same size, with lids or a saucer to cover them
tap water
cooking oil
salt
a small steel vessel and a stove, for boiling water
paper labels and a pen: A, B and C

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water and pours it. Let it cool until just warm before anyone touches the jar. Nails can be sharp at the tip.

schedule.what: Boil water for jar B. Set up the three jars. Make your guess. Look again after 3 hours.
Look at all three nails. Write and draw what you see.
Look again, take the nails out, and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each time you look. Draw each nail on day 3, colouring any rust orange.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Orange rust on much of the nail, orange flakes in the water
Still grey, one or two tiny spots

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three nails. 2. Ask them to guess which nail will rust most, and which least, and why.
flow.say: We'll put these iron nails in three jars of water. In one jar we'll keep oxygen away. Which nail do you think will rust most? Which will rust least? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the three nails. Which will rust most? Which will rust least? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason down before you start. Don't say what you expect. Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Boil about one glass of water in a small vessel for 5 minutes. 2. Put the lid on and let it cool for about 10 minutes, until warm.
flow.say: Boiling drives most of the air out of water. Air has oxygen in it. So boiled water has very little oxygen.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils some water. Boiling pushes the air out of it. So it has very little oxygen now.
flow.parent: Keep the lid on while it cools, so less air gets back in. You can set up jars A and C while it cools.

flow.do: 1. Label the jars A, B and C. 2. Fill jar A half full of tap water. 3. Fill jar C half full of tap water and stir in 1 teaspoon of salt. 4. Drop one nail into each.
flow.say: Jar A is plain water with air. Jar C is salty water with air, a bit like the sea.
flow.kid: Label the jars A, B and C. Put tap water in A. Put salty water in C. Drop a nail into each one.

flow.do: 1. Gently pour the warm boiled water into jar B, half full, without splashing. 2. Drop in the third nail. 3. Slowly pour 2 tablespoons of oil on top, so it makes a layer. 4. Put a lid on jar B.
flow.say: The oil layer stops air from getting back into the water. So the nail in jar B gets very little oxygen, like the iron in the young sea.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the boiled water into jar B. Drop in the nail. Pour oil on top. The oil keeps the air out.
flow.parent: Pour gently, because splashing mixes air back in. The oil should cover the whole surface. Put the three jars side by side, out of direct sun.

flow.do: After about 3 hours, look closely at each nail. Write what you see in the table.
flow.say: Let's look. Has anything changed yet?
flow.kid: Look at each nail closely. Any orange yet? Write it down.
flow.parent: The nail in salty water often shows an orange haze first. Tap water may show nothing yet. That is fine. Rust takes time.

flow.do: 1. Look at each nail on day 2. 2. Write and draw what you see. 3. Do not stir or move the jars.
flow.say: Which nail has changed most? Which has changed least?
flow.kid: Look at the nails again. Which one has the most orange? Which has none? Draw them.

check.q: In jar B, the nail sat in boiled water under a layer of oil. Why did the oil matter?
options: The oil kept air, with its oxygen, out of the water
check.why: Iron rusts when oxygen reaches it, and water helps. Boiling took most of the air out of the water, and the oil stopped air getting back in. Picking 'oil makes nails shiny' mixes up the oil layer with oiling a nail. Here the oil floats on top and does not touch the nail.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, look at all three nails. 2. Take them out with a spoon and lay them on a paper. 3. Compare them.
flow.say: Now let's see all three side by side. What do they tell us?
flow.kid: Take the nails out with a spoon. Lay them side by side. Which rusted most? Which least?
flow.parent: Usually C has rusted most, A has clear rust, and B is grey or has only a tiny spot or two. If B rusted a little, air got in, maybe from splashing or a gap in the oil. That is still a useful result: less oxygen gave less rust.

flow.do: Ask your child for three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: iron rusts when oxygen reaches it, and salt makes it rust faster. What I saw: nails A and C turned orange, but the nail in boiled water under oil stayed grey. Why: the oil kept oxygen away from nail B. Afterwards, tell them this. The young sea had almost no oxygen, so its iron did not rust. When microbes began making oxygen, the iron in the sea rusted and sank in layers.

check.q: Long ago, the sea had almost no oxygen. Then tiny microbes began making oxygen. What happened to the iron in the sea?
options: It joined with the oxygen, made rust and sank in layers
check.why: Your nail test showed that iron rusts where oxygen reaches it. In the sea, oxygen from microbes met the dissolved iron, and rust formed and settled on the sea floor. These layers became the red stripes in banded iron rock. Picking 'turned into microbes' mixes up the microbes with what their oxygen did.

setup.caption: 1. Three jars, three nails: open water, water under oil, salty water.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand pouring a thin stream of oil onto the water in jar B, making a yellow layer.
setup.caption: 2. Pour oil on jar B to keep the air out.

experiments.title: Banana Threads: can we see the instruction molecule?
experiments.context: In this experiment you break open the cells of a banana and pull out their DNA, the chain molecule that holds a living thing's instructions. You compare it with green peas, and with a glass that has no food at all.
experiments.question: Do a banana and green peas both hold white threads of DNA, and does a glass with no food give any?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you see anything in the glass with no food? Will the banana or the peas give more threads? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amounts of salt, washing liquid, water and spirit for every glass. Only the food changes: banana, green peas, or none.
results_table: What I saw in the spirit layer
How much (none, a little, a lot)

materials.item: half a ripe banana
2 tablespoons of green peas, fresh, frozen or soaked overnight
salt
dishwashing liquid
warm water, not hot
surgical spirit or rubbing alcohol from a medical shop, chilled in the freezer for 30 minutes
3 clear glasses or small glass jars
a tea strainer or a clean thin cotton cloth
2 small zip bags or bowls, and a spoon for mashing
a toothpick or wooden skewer

experiments.safety: Spirit catches fire easily and is poisonous to drink. A grown-up keeps the bottle, pours it, and keeps it far from the stove, lamps and flames. Wash hands afterwards. Don't eat anything used in the test.

schedule.what: Mash the foods, add salt and washing liquid, strain, add cold spirit, and look for white threads.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what you saw in each glass.

flow.do: 1. Put the spirit in the freezer 30 minutes before you start. 2. Show your child the banana, the peas and an empty glass. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Every cell holds a long chain molecule called DNA. It holds the instructions for that living thing. Do you think we can see it? Will the empty glass show anything? Why?
flow.kid: Every cell has instructions inside, in a chain called DNA. Can we see it? What will the empty glass show? Why?

flow.do: 1. Mix 1 cup warm water, 2 teaspoons salt and 4 teaspoons washing liquid. Stir gently, without making foam. 2. Mash the banana in one bag and the peas in another, with 2 spoons of the mix each, for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Mashing breaks the cells apart. The washing liquid breaks their thin skins. Salt helps the long DNA strands clump together, so we can see them.
flow.kid: Mash the banana well. Mash the peas well. You are breaking open millions of cells.
flow.parent: Keep the third portion of the mix with no food in it. That glass is the control. It shows what happens with no cells at all.

flow.do: 1. Add 4 more spoons of the mix to each bag. Squish gently for 1 minute. 2. Strain each one into its own glass, about a quarter full. 3. Pour the same amount of plain mix into the third glass.
flow.say: Now we strain out the lumps. The DNA is in the runny liquid now.
flow.kid: Strain each mash into its own glass. Pour plain mix into the third glass.

flow.do: 1. Tilt each glass. 2. Pour the cold spirit very slowly down the inside wall, until there is a layer as deep as the liquid below. 3. Stand the glasses still.
flow.say: Pour gently, so the spirit floats on top as its own layer. Don't stir.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours cold spirit slowly down the side. It floats on top. Don't shake the glass.
flow.parent: Pouring slowly is the most important step. If it mixes in, the threads are harder to see. Keep the spirit bottle closed and away from the stove.

flow.do: 1. Wait 3 to 5 minutes. 2. Look where the two layers meet. 3. Gently twirl the toothpick there in each glass.
flow.say: Look where the two layers meet. Can you see anything white and cloudy rising up?
flow.kid: Wait and watch where the layers meet. See white threads? Twirl the toothpick there.
flow.parent: White, cloudy, stringy stuff rises into the spirit layer in the banana and pea glasses. It winds onto the toothpick like wet cotton. The glass with no food stays clear. If you see little, the spirit may not be cold enough, or there may be too much liquid. Try again with less liquid and colder spirit.

check.q: The glass with no food stayed clear. The banana and pea glasses made white threads. What does this show?
options: The threads came from the salt and washing liquid
The threads came from the cells of the banana and the peas
The spirit makes threads by itself
check.why: All three glasses had the same salt, washing liquid and spirit, but only the glasses with food made threads. So the threads came from the cells. They are mostly DNA, millions of strands clumped together. Picking 'salt and washing liquid' is a fair guess, and that is exactly what the clear control glass tests.

flow.do: Ask for three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: banana and peas both have DNA in their cells. I saw white threads in both, and none in the glass with no food. The cells broke open and the DNA clumped in the cold spirit. Then tell them this. Your cells have DNA too, made of the same four kinds of letters. Every living thing uses this same chain. RNA is its close cousin, and many scientists think RNA came first.

setup.caption: 1. Mash the banana with salty, soapy water.

setup.caption: 2. A grown-up pours cold spirit slowly on top.

activities.title: The Chain of Mothers: who came before?
activities.context: This short activity opens the unit. You draw where you came from, going back and back, until you reach the biggest question in this unit.

materials.item: a long strip of paper, or two sheets taped end to end
pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Draw a chain of mothers going back in time, and ask what came first.

activities.record: Keep the drawing. You will add to it at the end of the unit.

flow.do: 1. At the right end of the strip, ask your child to draw themself. 2. To the left, draw their mother, then her mother.
flow.say: Draw yourself at this end. Who did you come from? Draw her next to you. And who did she come from?
flow.kid: Draw yourself at the right end. Draw your mother next to you. Then her mother.

flow.do: Keep going left with dotted lines, as far back as your child can imagine.
flow.say: Every living thing comes from another living thing. If we keep going back, and back, what do we reach?
flow.kid: Keep going back. Who came before her? And before that? Draw dots for the far past.
flow.parent: Children often draw cave people, then animals, then a fish. Let them. All are on the real path back. Don't correct the order now.

flow.do: At the far left end, draw a big question mark.
flow.say: Every living thing came from another living thing. So where did the very first one come from? That is what this unit is about.
flow.kid: Draw a big question mark at the far end. Who was first? Where did they come from?
flow.think: If life only comes from life, how could the first life begin?

activities.title: The Time String: 4.5 billion years along a corridor
activities.context: In this activity you make a timeline of the whole Earth to scale, using a string. One metre stands for one billion years. You see how long the Earth had only microbes.

materials.item: a string, ribbon or old saree border at least 4.5 metres long, or newspaper strips taped together
a measuring tape or a 30 cm ruler
8 paper labels, tape and a pen

activities.safety: Lay the string along the floor where nobody will trip on it.

schedule.what: Lay out the string and stick on labels for the big events in the story of life.

activities.record: Take a photo of the string, or draw it with the labels in order.

flow.do: 1. Lay the string straight along a corridor or across two rooms. 2. Mark one end 'Earth forms, 4.5 billion years ago' and the other 'Today'.
flow.say: Each metre is one billion years. This end is when the Earth formed. That end is today.
flow.kid: Lay the string straight. One end is when the Earth formed. The other end is today. Each metre is a billion years.

flow.do: 1. Measure from the Earth end. 2. Stick 'first oceans' at 10 cm and 'oldest stromatolites' at 1 metre. 3. Stick 'oxygen fills the air' at 2 metres 10 cm. 4. Stick 'Vempalle stromatolites in India' at 2 metres 50 cm.
flow.say: The oldest signs of life come one metre along. For the whole first metre, we have found no sure sign of life.
flow.kid: Measure and stick on each label. Where is the first life? How far from the start?
flow.parent: Children are often surprised that oxygen only fills the air halfway along. We have no sure fossils from the first metre, partly because very few rocks that old survive.

flow.do: 1. Now measure from the Today end. 2. Stick 'first animals' at 60 cm and 'dinosaurs die out' at 6.6 cm. 3. Make a pencil dot right at the end for 'first people'.
flow.say: Animals only appear in the last 60 centimetres. Dinosaurs died out about 6 and a half centimetres from the end. People are just the last pencil tip.
flow.kid: Measure from the Today end. Animals come 60 cm from the end. Where are people?

check.q: On the time string, one metre is one billion years. The string is 4.5 metres long. For how much of it was there only life too small to see, or no life at all?
options: About 3.9 metres, until the first animals
check.why: Animals appear about 60 cm from the Today end. Before that, for about 3.9 metres, the Earth had no life at all and then only microbes and other tiny living things. Picking 'only the last 60 cm' mixes up when animals came with when there was only tiny life.

flow.think: For most of the Earth's story, the only life was too small to see. What were they doing all that time?

activities.title: Copy the Chain: how RNA letters make a copy
activities.context: In this activity you use paper letter cards to see how a chain of RNA can be copied. The letters pair up, A with U and C with G, so a chain can make its own partner.

materials.item: 24 small squares of paper or card, with 6 each of A, U, C and G. Colour each letter its own colour.
a pencil

schedule.what: Make a chain, build its partner chain by the pairing rule, then copy the partner.

activities.record: Write your first chain, its partner and the partner's partner, one under the other.

flow.do: 1. Make the letter cards. 2. Write the rule on a paper: A pairs with U, C pairs with G.
flow.say: RNA is a chain made of four kinds of letters: A, U, C and G. A always pairs with U. C always pairs with G.
flow.kid: Make your letter cards. Remember the rule. A pairs with U. C pairs with G.

flow.do: Lay down a chain of 6 letters in a row, in any order you like.
flow.say: Make a chain of six letters. Any order you like. That order is your message.
flow.kid: Lay six letters in a row, any order. That is your chain.

flow.do: Under each letter, lay its partner, to make a second chain.
flow.say: Now make the partner chain. Under each A put a U, under each U an A, under each C a G, under each G a C.
flow.kid: Under each letter, put its partner. A goes with U. C goes with G.

check.q: A chain reads A C G U. Which is its partner chain?
check.why: A pairs with U, C with G, G with C, and U with A. So A C G U has the partner U G C A. Picking 'A C G U' means copying the letters straight, but the chain is copied by partners, not by the same letters.

flow.do: Now make the partner of the partner chain, under it. Compare it with the first chain.
flow.say: Now make a partner for the partner. What do you notice when you compare it with your first chain?
flow.kid: Make a partner for the partner chain. Look at your first chain. What do you see?
flow.parent: The third chain matches the first exactly. That is how a chain can be copied: partner, then partner again. In cells, proteins help with this copying. In the RNA idea, the first RNA chains copied themselves with help only from chemicals around them, and maybe from other RNA.

setup.art: Coloured paper squares with the letters A, U, C and G spread on a table, and a note saying A–U, C–G.
setup.caption: 1. Make letter cards and write the pairing rule.

setup.art: Three rows of letter cards one under another: A C G U A G, then U G C A U C, then A C G U A G.
setup.caption: 2. Build the partner, then the partner's partner.

activities.title: Copy Mistakes: how one chain becomes many
activities.context: In this activity you copy a chain of letters again and again, each time from your last copy, with a timer running. You count how the chain slowly changes.

materials.item: a paper and pencil
a phone or clock with a timer

schedule.what: Copy a 12-letter chain 8 times, fast, each from the last copy. Count the changes.

activities.record: Keep all the copies in a column. Circle every letter that is different from the first chain.

flow.do: Write this chain at the top of the paper: A U G C C A U G G A C U.
flow.say: Here is a chain of 12 letters. You will copy it eight times, but each copy is made from the copy before.
flow.kid: Write this chain at the top. You will copy it eight times.

flow.do: 1. Give 10 seconds for each copy. 2. Each copy goes under the last one, copied only from the last one. 3. Cover the older lines with a hand.
flow.say: Ten seconds for each copy. Go! Only look at the line just above.
flow.kid: Copy the line above in 10 seconds. Cover the older lines. Go fast!
flow.parent: Fast copying gives some mistakes, which is the point. If there are no mistakes at all, try 6 seconds a copy.

flow.do: Compare the last copy with the first chain. Circle every letter that changed.
flow.say: How many letters changed? Did a mistake, once made, carry on into the next copies?
flow.kid: Circle every letter that changed. Did a mistake stay in the copies after it?

check.q: In the copying game, a mistake in copy 3 was still there in copies 4 to 8. Why?
options: Each copy was made from the copy before, so the mistake was copied too
check.why: Each copy is made from the one before it. So a change, once made, is passed on to every later copy. This is how changes add up in living things over many generations. Picking 'mistakes disappear' is a common guess, but a mistake is fixed only if someone checks the copy against the first chain.

flow.think: Living cells copy their DNA with a checker that fixes most mistakes. Why might it be good to keep a few?

activities.title: Find a Living Film (in the monsoon, or by a damp corner)
activities.context: This activity is for when you can find a damp wall, an old flowerpot or a wet drain cover. The green or black film on them often holds cyanobacteria and algae, cousins of the microbes that built the oldest stromatolites and first made oxygen.

materials.item: a damp wall, flowerpot or tank lid with a green or black film
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in

activities.safety: Look, don't lick. Wash hands after touching. Stay away from roads and deep drains.

schedule.what: Find a green or black film, look at it closely, and photograph or draw it.

activities.record: Draw or photograph the film. Write where you found it and whether it was in sun or shade.

flow.do: Look for a green or black slimy film on a damp wall, the outside of a clay pot, or a balcony drain.
flow.say: This green film is made of millions of tiny living things. Some of them make oxygen, like the microbes that built the oldest rocks.
flow.kid: Look for a green or black film on something damp. It is millions of tiny living things.
flow.parent: In the monsoon this is easy to find, especially on north-facing walls and old pots. In a dry season, look near a dripping tap or AC outlet. If you cannot find one, look at photos of Shark Bay stromatolites instead.

flow.do: Look through the magnifying glass, or zoom in with a phone camera.
flow.say: Can you see single living things? Or only a carpet? That carpet is called a mat.
flow.kid: Zoom in with the lens or the phone. Can you see one microbe? Or a carpet?
flow.parent: You won't see single cells, which are far too small. You may see threads or a velvety surface. A carpet of microbes like this is what built stromatolites.

flow.do: Draw or photograph it, and write where you found it.
flow.say: Is it in the sun or the shade? Why might that matter to living things that make food from light?
flow.kid: Draw it. Was it in sun or shade? Write it down.

activities.title: Where Did Life Begin? A debate with evidence
activities.context: In this activity you weigh up three ideas about where life began: hot vents on the sea floor, warm pools on land, or space. Nobody knows the answer, so you argue from the evidence.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, one for each idea
pencils

schedule.what: Read the evidence for three ideas, argue for one, then argue against it.

activities.record: Write which idea you think is best, and your best reason.

flow.do: Write one idea at the top of each sheet: sea-floor vents, warm pools on land, from space. Under each, write the evidence from the explanation card 'Where did life begin?'.
flow.say: Nobody knows where life began. Scientists argue about three main ideas. Let's write down the evidence for each.
flow.kid: Write one idea on each paper. Under each, write what supports it.

flow.do: Your child picks one idea and argues for it for one minute. Then you argue against it for one minute.
flow.say: Pick the idea you think is best. Tell me why. Then I'll try to argue against it.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Tell why it is best. Then hear the other side.
flow.parent: For vents: warmth, minerals and energy all the time. Against: chains break in hot water. For pools: drying helps chains join. Against: little dry land then. For space: meteorites carry amino acids. Against: it doesn't explain how life began out there.

flow.do: Swap: now your child argues against their own idea. Then they say which idea they think best now, and why.
flow.say: Now argue against your own idea. Did you change your mind?
flow.kid: Now argue against your own idea. Do you still think the same? Why?

check.q: Which of these is true about where life began?
options: Scientists know it began at sea-floor vents
Scientists know it came from space
Nobody knows yet, and scientists are testing several ideas
check.why: There is evidence for each idea, but none is proven. Picking a single place usually comes from hearing one idea told as if it were settled. Good scientists say 'nobody knows yet' when that is true.

setup.caption: 1. Three ideas, one sheet each, with the evidence.

setup.art: A girl standing and arguing, with her mother listening and holding up a finger to answer.
setup.caption: 2. Argue for an idea, then against it.

projects.title: The Story of Life, Told by RNA: make a picture book
projects.context: In this 3-day project you make a short picture book in which RNA tells the story of life, from the young sea to you. It has to be true, and where nobody knows, it has to say so.

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper folded in half and stapled, to make an 8-page book
pencils, crayons or paints
a picture book about the story of life, if you have one

schedule.what: Plan 6 pages: the young Earth, the building blocks, RNA copying, the first cell skins, stromatolites, and the first oxygen.
Draw and write each page, with one or two sentences in RNA's own voice.
Add a last page, 'What nobody knows yet', and read the book aloud to your family.

projects.record: The finished book. On the back, list one thing in it that scientists know and one thing that is still an idea.

flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the book. 2. Together, list 6 page titles. 3. For each page, your child says one true sentence.
flow.say: RNA is telling the story. What happened first? What came next? Let's list six pages.
flow.kid: Make your book. Plan six pages. What does RNA say on each one?
flow.parent: Help with order: young Earth and sea, building blocks forming, RNA chains copying, chains inside fatty bubbles, stromatolites, oxygen rusting the sea. Keep each sentence true. Where it is only an idea, RNA can say 'Many scientists think...'.

flow.do: Draw and write each page.
flow.say: Draw each page and write RNA's words. Keep it true.
flow.kid: Draw each page. Write what RNA says. Is each sentence true?

check.q: On one page, RNA says 'I was the very first life, for certain.' Is that a good sentence for a true book?
options: No, it should say many scientists think so, but it is still being tested
Yes, because RNA is in every cell
check.why: The RNA idea is a hypothesis. It has good evidence but is not proven. Picking 'RNA is in every cell' is a fair reason to like the idea, but it does not prove RNA came first.

flow.do: 1. Add the last page, 'What nobody knows yet'. 2. Your child reads the book aloud to the family.
flow.say: What is the biggest thing nobody knows yet? Put it on the last page. Then read us your book.
flow.kid: Write the last page: what nobody knows yet. Read your book to your family.

challenges.title: Keep the Nail Grey
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that follows the nail test. You find a way to stop an iron nail from rusting for three days, even though it sits in open tap water.
challenges.problem: An iron nail in open tap water rusts within a day or two. Find a way to keep a nail grey for three days in open water, using things from home.
constraints: The nail must sit in open tap water, with no lid and no oil layer on the water.
Put an untreated nail in another jar beside it, so you can compare.
materials: coatings to try: cooking oil, ghee, coconut oil, candle wax, nail polish, petroleum jelly, crayon
general: Coat the nail with grease or petroleum jelly, so water and air can't touch the iron.
Paint it with nail polish, as iron gates are painted.
Dip it in melted candle wax, with a grown-up.
creative: Wrap the nail tightly in a strip of aluminium foil. Aluminium may protect the iron, a little like the zinc coat on shiny nails.
Rub the nail with a crayon until it is covered in wax.
Test which coating lasts longest when you rub the nail a little each day.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own way to keep a nail grey. Test it against an untreated nail for three days. Which worked best, and why?

flow.do: Remind your child of the nail test. Ask what a nail needs in order to rust.
flow.say: In the nail test, what did a nail need in order to rust?
flow.kid: What does a nail need to rust? Think back to the jars.
flow.parent: Iron needs oxygen and water to rust. So any coat that keeps both away should work.

flow.do: Draw three ideas for keeping water and air away from the nail.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. Draw three ways to keep the nail grey.
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. How can you keep water and air off the nail?

flow.do: 1. Coat one nail with the best idea. 2. Put it in a glass of tap water. 3. Put an uncoated nail in another glass beside it. 4. Check over three days.
flow.say: Now test it. We'll compare your coated nail with a plain one.
flow.kid: Coat one nail. Put both nails in water. Check them for three days.
flow.parent: Melted wax needs a grown-up and a low flame or a candle. Nail polish and petroleum jelly are easiest.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions, then invent one more.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you think of a better one?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ones. Invent your own.
flow.think: The iron in the young sea had no coat. What kept it from rusting for so long?

challenges.title: The Copying Machine
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that follows the copy-mistakes activity. You invent a way to copy a 20-letter chain fast, with as few mistakes as possible.
challenges.problem: Copy a 20-letter chain of A, U, C and G five times, each copy from the last, in under one minute per copy. Invent a way to make fewer mistakes.
constraints: Each copy must take less than one minute.
Each copy is made from the copy before.
Count the mistakes in the fifth copy.
materials: letter cards from the Copy the Chain activity
a family member as a helper
general: Copy in groups of 4 letters at a time, so you don't lose your place.
After each copy, check it against the line above.
Use a ruler under the line you are copying.
creative: Have a helper check each copy, like the checker in a cell that fixes mistakes.
Copy by partners instead, A to U and C to G, then partner again, so each letter is checked twice.
Give each letter a colour, so a wrong letter stands out.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own copying machine. Test it: how many mistakes in the fifth copy, compared with copying fast with no method?

flow.do: Write a 20-letter chain. Copy it five times fast, with no method, and count the mistakes.
flow.say: First, let's see how many mistakes we make with no method at all.
flow.kid: Copy the chain five times, fast. Count the mistakes in the last copy.

flow.do: Draw or list three ideas for copying with fewer mistakes.
flow.say: How could you copy with fewer mistakes, and still be quick?
flow.kid: Think of three ways to make fewer mistakes. Write them down.

flow.do: Try the best idea. Copy five times again and count the mistakes.
flow.say: Test your best idea. Did you make fewer mistakes this time?
flow.kid: Try your best idea. Copy five times. Count the mistakes again.
flow.parent: Checking each copy against the one above usually cuts mistakes the most. Living cells do this too: some of their copying proteins check and fix mistakes.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas, then invent one more.
flow.say: Here are some ideas. Which would you add to your machine?
flow.kid: Read the ideas. Which one would you add?
flow.think: If the first RNA copied with no checker, it made many mistakes. Was that good or bad for life?
