quiz.p: Every living thing comes from another living thing. Why does that make the first life a puzzle?
quiz.why: If life only comes from life, then the first life had nothing alive to come from. So something must once have been different.
opts: Because there are too many living things
Because the first life had no living thing to come from

quiz.p: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. About how old are the oldest signs of life we are fairly sure of?
quiz.why: About 3.5 billion years, from stromatolites in Western Australia. Picking 4.5 billion would mean life began the moment the Earth formed.

quiz.p: On a time string where 1 metre is 1 billion years, how far from the start are the oldest stromatolites, from 3.5 billion years ago?
quiz.why: 4.5 minus 3.5 is 1. So the oldest stromatolites are 1 metre from the start.
Mud settled on a mat of microbes, and the microbes grew up through it to make a new mat. Layer after layer built a dome. Picking 'carried stones' gives microbes a job they cannot do at their size.
opts: Mud settled on their mat, and they grew up through it, again and again

quiz.p: Revathi puts an iron nail in boiled water, pours oil on top and closes the lid. Another nail sits in open tap water. After three days, what will she most likely see?
quiz.why: The nail in open water rusts, because oxygen reaches it. The nail sealed under oil gets very little oxygen, so it stays almost grey.
opts: The open-water nail rusty, the sealed nail almost grey
The sealed nail rusty, the open-water nail grey

quiz.p: What do the red stripes in banded iron rock show?
quiz.why: They are layers of rust that formed when oxygen made by microbes met iron in the sea.
opts: Rust that formed when oxygen from microbes met iron in the sea

quiz.p: A chain of RNA reads C A G U. What is its partner chain?
quiz.why: C pairs with G, A with U, G with C, and U with A. So the partner is G U C A.

quiz.p: What does the RNA idea say?
quiz.why: It says that the first life may have been RNA, which can carry instructions and do jobs. DNA and proteins came later. It is still being tested.
opts: The first life may have been RNA that could help copy itself
RNA is a kind of rock

quiz.p: Why do scientists call the RNA idea a hypothesis and not a fact?
quiz.why: It has good evidence, but nobody has yet shown RNA copying itself from scratch, as the idea needs.
opts: Because it has not yet been fully shown to work

quiz.p: What did Stanley Miller's spark experiment show?
quiz.why: It showed that amino acids, building blocks of proteins, can form from water and simple gases with energy, without any living thing.
opts: Building blocks of life can form without living things
Life can be made in a week

quiz.p: Before 1828, many chemists believed something that Wöhler showed was wrong. What was it?
quiz.why: They believed only living things could make the chemicals of life. Wöhler made urea from non-living chemicals.
opts: That only living things could make the chemicals of life
That RNA was the first life

quiz.p: Which is true about where life began?
quiz.why: Vents, warm pools and space all have supporters and evidence, but nobody knows yet.
opts: It began at sea-floor vents, for certain
It began in warm pools, for certain
It came from space, for certain

quiz.p: In the banana test, white threads rose into the cold spirit. What were they?
quiz.why: They were mostly DNA, the chain molecule that holds the instructions in every cell, clumped together in millions of strands.
opts: Mostly DNA from the banana's cells

items.p: About how old is the Earth?
items.why: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Picking 4,500 years is a common mix-up between thousands and billions.

items.p: How old are the oldest signs of life we are fairly sure of?
items.why: Stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old, in Western Australia, are the oldest signs of life most scientists accept.

items.p: Every living thing today comes from another living thing.
items.why: True. Puppies come from dogs, plants from seeds, and bacteria from other bacteria.

items.p: Scientists know for sure how life began.
items.why: False. Nobody knows yet. There are good ideas, such as the RNA idea, and scientists are testing them.

items.p: A rock built in thin layers by mats of microbes is called a ____.
items.why: Stromatolites grow as microbe mats trap mud and grow up through it, layer after layer.

items.p: In the nail test, which nail stayed grey the longest?
items.why: The nail in boiled water under oil got very little oxygen, so it hardly rusted. The salty water nail rusted fastest.
opts: The nail in open tap water
The nail in boiled water under oil
The nail in open salty water

items.p: Iron joins with ____ to make rust.
items.why: Rust forms when oxygen reaches iron, and water helps.

items.p: Match each RNA letter to its partner.
items.why: A pairs with U, and C pairs with G.

items.p: A chain reads A A C G. Write its partner chain.
items.why: A pairs with U, and C pairs with G. So A A C G has the partner U U G C.

items.p: What did the first oxygen made by microbes do to the iron in the sea?
items.why: Oxygen met the dissolved iron and made rust, which sank in layers. These became banded iron rocks.
opts: It made rust, which sank in layers
It turned the iron into salt

items.p: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things that use sunlight.
items.why: True. Cyanobacteria, algae and plants give out oxygen when they make food from sunlight.

items.p: Put these in order, oldest first.
items.why: The Earth formed 4.5 billion years ago, the oldest stromatolites are about 3.5 billion years old, oxygen filled the air from about 2.4 billion years ago, the first animals came about 600 million years ago, and people only about 300,000 years ago.

items.p: What is RNA?
items.why: RNA is a chain molecule with four kinds of letters: A, U, C and G. It is a close cousin of DNA.
opts: A chain molecule of four kinds of letters

items.p: Draw a stromatolite cut open, and show its layers.
items.a: A dome of rock with many thin wavy layers, one on top of the other.
items.why: Each layer was once a mat of microbes that grew up through the mud on top of it.

items.p: Sort these: living thing, or once made by living things?
items.why: Cyanobacteria and a curd bacterium are alive now. A stromatolite, banded iron rock and the oxygen in the air were made by living things.

items.p: Stanley Miller filled a flask with water and gases and made sparks in it for a week. What did he find?
items.why: He found amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. This showed they can form without living things.

items.p: Before 1828, many chemists believed the chemicals of living bodies could be made only by...
items.why: They believed only living things, with a 'life force', could make them. Wöhler made urea from non-living chemicals and showed this was wrong.

items.p: Friedrich Wöhler made ____, a chemical found in urine, from non-living chemicals.
items.why: In 1828 he made urea from ammonium cyanate.

items.p: Why is the RNA idea attractive to scientists?
items.why: RNA can both carry instructions, like DNA, and do some jobs, like proteins. So it could have come first.
opts: Because RNA is found only in meteorites
Because RNA can carry instructions and also do some jobs

items.p: The RNA idea has been proven in the lab.
items.why: False. Scientists have made parts of it work, such as RNA that copies other RNA, but not RNA that copies itself from scratch.

items.p: In the banana test, the glass with no food stayed clear. Why was that glass useful?
items.why: It is the control. It showed that the threads came from the cells, not from the salt, washing liquid or spirit.
opts: It made the banana taste better
It showed the threads came from the cells, not the other things

items.p: Why did we boil the water for jar B in the nail test?
items.a: Boiling drives most of the air, with its oxygen, out of the water.
items.why: With little oxygen in the water, the nail could hardly rust.

items.p: What is a ribozyme?
items.why: A ribozyme is a piece of RNA that does a job, like cutting or joining other molecules.

items.p: The part of the ribosome that joins amino acids into proteins is made of ____.
items.why: This was shown in 2000. It is one of the strongest clues for the RNA idea.

items.p: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize for working out the shape of the ribosome, was born in which town?
items.why: He was born in Chidambaram, in Tamil Nadu. He shared the prize with Ada Yonath and Thomas Steitz.

items.p: Fatty acid molecules can form tiny hollow bubbles in water by themselves.
items.why: True. Their water-shy ends tuck in, and they close up into bubbles. The first cell skins may have formed this way.

items.p: Why are living stromatolites found at Shark Bay in Australia?
items.why: The water there is very salty, and few snails and other grazers can live in it to eat the microbe mats.
opts: The water is so salty that few grazers can eat the mats

items.p: Copy this chain twice by partners: G U U A. What is the second copy?
items.why: The first partner is C A A U. Its partner is G U U A, the same as the start.

items.p: In the copy-mistakes activity, why did a mistake carry on into all the later copies?
items.why: Each copy was made from the one before, so a change was passed on.
opts: Each copy was made from the one before

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A, U, C, G, T
items.why: A, U, C and G are the letters of RNA. T is used in DNA in place of U.

items.p: Give one piece of evidence for the idea that life began at hot sea-floor vents, and one problem with it.
items.a: For: vents give warmth, minerals and energy all the time. Against: long chains like RNA break apart easily in hot water.
items.why: Both sides have evidence, which is why scientists still argue.

items.p: Give one piece of evidence for the idea that life began in warm pools on land, and one problem with it.
items.a: For: drying and wetting helps small molecules join into chains. Against: there was little dry land on the young Earth.
items.why: Again, there is evidence on both sides.

items.p: Some say life came to Earth from space. What is the biggest problem with this as an answer to how life began?
items.why: Even if life came from space, it still had to begin somewhere. The idea moves the question, but does not answer it.
opts: It does not explain how life began out there

items.p: In the nail test, Divya's nail in jar B rusted a little on day 3. Give one reason this might have happened.
items.a: Some air got into the water: from splashing while pouring, a gap in the oil layer, or air dissolving back in while it cooled.
items.why: An odd result is a clue. Less oxygen still gave much less rust than in jars A and C.

items.p: Long ago, iron could stay dissolved in the sea for a very long time. Why?
items.why: There was almost no oxygen in the sea to turn the iron into rust.
opts: There was almost no oxygen to make rust
The iron was hidden in fish

items.p: All living things today use DNA, RNA and ribosomes.
items.why: True. This is one of the main reasons scientists think all life shares one family.

items.p: If a chain of RNA could copy itself in the sea, would you call it alive? Give a reason.
items.a: Any answer with a reason. For example: yes, because it makes copies of itself and can change. Or: no, because it has no skin and does not take in food.
items.why: Scientists themselves disagree on where to draw the line between chemistry and life.

items.p: Why is it hard to find fossils of the very first life?
items.why: Very few rocks older than about 3.5 billion years survive, and the first life was tiny and soft.
opts: Very few rocks that old survive, and the first life was tiny and soft
The first life was made of iron

items.p: Proteins are needed to copy DNA, and DNA is needed to make proteins. Explain why this is a puzzle, and how the RNA idea tries to solve it.
items.a: Each needs the other, so it is hard to see which came first. RNA can carry instructions and do jobs, so RNA could have come first, before both.
items.why: This is like the chicken and the egg. The RNA idea says the first life used one molecule for both jobs.

items.p: Zita Martins and her team found uracil in the Murchison meteorite. Why does this matter?
items.why: Uracil is one of the four letters of RNA. Finding it in a meteorite shows that RNA letters can form in space, without life.
opts: It shows that an RNA letter can form without life
It shows the meteorite came from India
It shows the meteorite was alive

items.p: Kavya says: 'Oxygen was always in the air.' What would you tell her, using the nail test and banded iron rock?
items.a: Iron rusts where oxygen reaches it. The young sea held dissolved iron without rusting, so it had little oxygen. Red rust layers in banded iron show when oxygen made by microbes arrived.
items.why: Rocks older than about 2.4 billion years show almost no oxygen in the air.

items.p: Which of these is NOT evidence that all life is one family?
items.why: All life using DNA, ribosomes and the same code points to one family. Being green does not: many living things are not green.
opts: All life reads the same genetic code

items.p: On a time string where 1 metre is 1 billion years, how far from the Today end are the first animals, from about 600 million years ago?
items.why: 600 million is 6 tenths of a billion. 6 tenths of a metre is 60 centimetres.

items.p: Ask one question about how life began that you think nobody has answered yet.
items.a: Any honest question. For example: what was the first RNA chain? Did life begin more than once?
items.why: Open questions drive science. Good ones can be tested.

items.p: Draw what you think the first cell looked like: a skin, and something inside that could be copied.
items.a: A round bubble with a thin skin and a short chain of letters inside.
items.why: Many scientists think the first cells were fatty acid bubbles with RNA inside.

applications: Searching for life on Mars: the Perseverance rover is collecting rock samples from Jezero Crater, an old lake bed, to look for signs of ancient microbes.
Space missions to the icy moons Europa and Enceladus, which have oceans under their ice, look for the chemistry life might need.
mRNA vaccines, such as some COVID-19 vaccines, use RNA to give cells instructions. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize for the work behind them.
Some antibiotics, such as streptomycin and tetracycline, work by jamming the ribosomes of bacteria.
Painting, oiling and coating iron, such as gates, bridges and ship hulls, keeps oxygen and water away so it rusts less.
Geologists use stromatolites and banded iron rocks to find limestone, phosphate and iron ore. Jhamarkotra in Rajasthan is a phosphate mine near stromatolites.
DNA tests in hospitals and in forensic labs start with pulling DNA out of cells, as the banana test does.
Chemists who study how life began help design new ways to make medicines and materials from simple chemicals.

open_questions.why_open: There are good ideas, but nobody has made life from non-living chemicals, and the first life left no fossils we have found.
RNA can carry instructions and do jobs, but it is hard to make without a cell and breaks easily. Some scientists think other chemistry came first.

open_questions.q: Where did life begin: at sea-floor vents, in warm pools on land, or somewhere else?
open_questions.why_open: Each place has evidence for and against. There are no rocks left from the exact time and place.
The oldest sure signs are about 3.5 billion years old. Some scientists think life is older, but older rocks are rare and changed by heat.

open_questions.q: Did life begin once, or many times?
open_questions.why_open: All life today is one family. Other kinds may have begun and died out without a trace.

open_questions.q: Is there life on other worlds?
open_questions.why_open: No life has been found beyond Earth yet. Mars, Europa and Enceladus are being studied.

open_questions.q: How did the genetic code, the rules for turning RNA letters into proteins, begin?
open_questions.why_open: All life uses nearly the same code, but nobody knows how it first came about.

maths.problem: On the time string, 1 metre stands for 1 billion years. The oldest stromatolites are from 3.5 billion years ago. How far from the Today end do they go?
maths.explain: Each billion years is 1 metre. So 3.5 billion years is 3.5 metres. 0.5 of a metre is 50 centimetres. So it is 3 metres and 50 centimetres from the Today end. That is 1 metre from the start, because 4.5 minus 3.5 is 1.
maths.context: This is about the Time String. You lay a 4.5 metre string along the floor, with one metre for each billion years.
maths.why_maths: A billion years is too long to imagine. Turning years into metres lets you see how long life has been here.

maths.problem: On the time string, 1 centimetre stands for 10 million years. Dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago. About how far from the Today end should that label go? Is it nearer 6 cm or 7 cm?
maths.answer: About 6.6 centimetres, a little nearer 7 cm.
maths.explain: 66 million years is 6 lots of 10 million, and 6 million more. 6 lots make 6 cm. 6 million is 6 tenths of 10 million, so it is about 6 tenths of a centimetre more. 6.6 cm is nearer 7 than 6.
maths.context: This is about the Time String, where 1 metre is 1 billion years, so 1 centimetre is 10 million years.
maths.why_maths: A scale model only works if you change every date by the same rule. Then you can compare times by looking.

maths.problem: You make the 4.5 metre time string from newspaper strips, each 50 centimetres long. How many strips do you need?
maths.explain: Two strips of 50 cm make 1 metre. 4 metres need 4 lots of 2, which is 8 strips. Half a metre more needs 1 more strip. 8 plus 1 is 9.
maths.context: This is about making the Time String from newspaper if you have no long string.
maths.why_maths: Working out the strips first means you cut just enough paper and the timeline comes out the right length.

maths.problem: Meenakshi counted rust spots on her nails after 2 days. The nail in open tap water had 10 spots. The nail in salty water had 30. The nail under oil had 1. How many times as many spots did the salty-water nail have as the tap-water nail? What does this tell you?
maths.answer: 3 times as many. Salt makes iron rust faster.
maths.explain: 30 divided by 10 is 3, so the salty-water nail had 3 times as many spots. Both nails had air and water. The only difference was salt, so salt made the rust form faster. The nail under oil had far fewer spots than either, because little oxygen reached it.
maths.context: This is about the Rusting Nails test, with nails in open tap water, in salty water, and in boiled water under oil.
maths.why_maths: Saying '3 times as many' shows how big the difference is, which a plain 'more' does not.

maths.problem: Imagine one RNA chain that makes one copy of itself every hour, and every copy does the same. Start with 1 chain. How many chains are there after 5 hours?
maths.explain: The number doubles every hour: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. After 1 hour there are 2, and after 5 hours there are 32. Doubling grows very fast. After 10 hours there would be 1,024.
maths.context: This is about the RNA idea, where chains of RNA make copies of themselves.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the doubling pattern shows why something that copies itself can fill a sea, even from one chain.

roots.context: We have learned about the oldest life, the first oxygen, and the RNA idea of how life began. Now we ask what this story tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your nail in open water rusted, but the nail sealed under oil stayed almost grey. Iron rusts only where oxygen reaches it. Earth's early sea had almost no oxygen until tiny microbes began making it. Their oxygen rusted iron in the sea, and much of that rust became the iron ore India mines today.
deep_truth.habit: We think of the Earth as a stage, and living things as the actors who live on it. But the oldest life changed the stage itself: the air, the sea and the rocks. The planet we live on is partly made by life.
deep_truth.evidence: In the nail test, the nail with oxygen rusted and the nail without oxygen did not. Banded iron rocks, at Kudremukh, Sandur and Bailadila, hold red layers of rust that formed when oxygen made by microbes met iron in the sea.

three.who_am_i: Your cells hold DNA and RNA written in the same four-letter way as a banana's and a microbe's. You come from the same first cells as every living thing.
three.what_is_life: Life began small and stayed tiny for most of the Earth's story. Those tiny lives changed the sea, the rocks and the air.
three.what_is_this_world: The air you breathe, and even the iron in a nail, carry the work of microbes from billions of years ago.

roots.thread: Before life, the young sea held only a few kinds of simple molecules. Some joined into chains, and chains that could be copied made more of themselves. Small copying mistakes made new kinds, and those made more kinds still. From a few simple molecules came every living thing, from microbes to mango trees to you. And the living things, in turn, remade the sea, the air and the rocks they came from.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many chemists thought the chemicals in living bodies were special. They believed only a living thing, with a 'life force' inside it, could make them. In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler, a German chemist, heated a salt called ammonium cyanate, which is made from non-living chemicals. To his surprise, he got urea, a chemical found in urine. He wrote to a friend that he had made urea without needing a kidney. It took many more experiments to convince everyone, but the old idea began to crack. More than a hundred years later, in 1952, Stanley Miller was a young student working with Harold Urey in Chicago. He wanted to test an idea of Alexander Oparin in Russia and J.B.S. Haldane in Britain: that the young sea was a soup in which life's chemicals could form. He filled a flask with water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen, and made electric sparks in it for a week. The water turned brown. In it were amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Haldane later moved to India and became an Indian citizen. He worked in Kolkata and Bhubaneswar until he died in 1964.
how_we_found_out.who: Friedrich Wöhler, a German chemist, and Stanley Miller, an American student working with Harold Urey
how_we_found_out.when: 1828 (Wöhler makes urea) and 1952 (Miller's spark experiment, published in 1953)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought that the chemicals of living things could only be made by living things, with a special life force. Wöhler made urea from non-living chemicals, and Miller made amino acids from gases, water and sparks.
